newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T profits rise 5 percent, despite charge for U.S. unit.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T profits rise 5 percent, despite charge for U.S. unit.

text.p: B.A.T Industries Plc said Wednesday that its profits grew by 5 percent last year despite a charge of 160 million pounds ($258.5 million) for environmental claims against a U.S. insurance unit.

The big diversified company, which is involved in industries ranging from tobacco to insurance, said its 1996 profits rose to 2.495 billion pounds ($4 billion), despite the exceptional charge for claims against its Eagle Star insurance unit. Excluding the charge, profits rose by 7 percent.
Chairman Lord Cairns said in a statement that the company denied any liability for damages currently being claimed by smokers in a string of tobacco related lawsuits in the United States.

"We continue to believe that B.A.T Industries itself has no potential liability in any U.S. tobacco litigation," Cairns said, adding that the tobacco industry was confident of winning the cases and does not intend to offer a settlement.
However, Cairns said the company would be prepared to "evaluate proposals from third parties to provide relief from all current and future suits, provided that they were in shareholders' interests."

The company also said it had an open mind on its corporate structure, but declined to reveal any concrete plans. Some analysts had hoped B.A.T would say more about a possible split up of its tobacco and insurance arms.

The company has looked at several options for improving shareholder return over the past year, including merging its financial services arm, comprising mainly general and life insurance companies, with another insurer.
"We are not convinced that simply doing the splits helps either business much," Director of Public Affairs Michael Prideaux said.

Prideaux dismissed the idea of spinning off the company's U.S. cigarette arm, Brown & Williamson, as a way of protecting the rest of B.A.T from any potential liability to smokers in the United States.

B.A.T's tobacco business turned in a 7 percent overall improvement in local currency terms to 1.634 billion pounds ($2.64 billion) with sales 4 percent ahead and world market share increasing to 12.8 percent from 12.4 percent.

Trading profit from financial services grew by an underlying 8 percent to 1.2 billion ($1.94 billion) with strong performances from two insurers, Farmers in the United States and Allied Dunbar in Britain.
